findings: Auth placement matches the report's expectations and is consistently header-based for the two media-server auth schemes: Plex sends bare X-Plex-Token, Emby sends bare X-Emby-Token, Jellyfin sends 'Authorization: MediaBrowser Token="…"' — all set via MediaServerKind.authHeaders(token:) (MediaServerConfig.swift:38-50), never in a query string, for every one of the 8 protocol methods on both clients.

TMDB is the one place a secret CAN travel in the query string: TMDBClient.get() (TMDBClient.swift:588-618) appends api_key= to the query for a legacy v3 hex key (only when the pasted credential is not a v4 JWT, detected by isReadAccessToken()). This only applies to the JSON API calls (api.themoviedb.org/3/...), never to image URLs (image.tmdb.org, no auth needed at all) — so no TMDB image URL ever carries a key.

The TMDB v3-key-in-query URLs are never persisted or hashed into a cache key: TMDBClient's get() is private and only decoded JSON model values (not the raw URL) leave the function, so the api_key never reaches PosterStore, title-metadata.json, or QueueItem. No leak found in this codebase today.

PosterStore's design explicitly documents and defends against the leak the task asks about: media-server poster URLs are built token-free by PlexClient/JellyfinClient (comment at MediaServerPosterAccess.swift:6-13 and PlexClient.swift:248-250 / JellyfinClient.swift:299), and PosterStore.download() re-attaches the media-server token per-request as a header via MediaServerPosterAccess.shared.headers(for:) rather than baking it into the URL. The disk/memory cache key (PosterStore.key(for:), line 519-522) is SHA256(url.absoluteString) — a one-way hash, not the raw URL — so even a URL that did carry a secret would not be recoverable from the cache key or filename. No credential leak found in PosterStore.

DemoMode.isActive is NOT checked inside PlexClient, JellyfinClient, MediaServerIndex, TMDBClient, PosterStore, or LocalToolBackend+TMDB.swift — none of those files reference DemoMode at all. The only demo-mode short-circuit found in this scope is in SeriesIdentityResolver.swift (lines 73 and 89: 'guard tmdbTVId > 0, !DemoMode.isActive, ...'), which gates the TMDB/Sonarr identity-resolution bridge but not the media-server clients or the TMDB catalog/discover calls used elsewhere (e.g. LocalToolBackend+TMDB.swift's tmdbDiscoverMovies/tmdbDiscoverSeries construct a live TMDBClient unconditionally).

MediaKit's MediaServerProvider.request() (Providers/MediaServerProvider.swift:178-197) collapses the Jellyfin/Emby auth branch into a single 'MediaBrowser Token="…"' header for both, unlike the shipping ArrCore MediaServerKind.authHeaders which sends a bare X-Emby-Token for Emby and only wraps the token in the MediaBrowser scheme for Jellyfin. This is a behavior discrepancy the spike would need to reconcile before replacing JellyfinClient — a real Emby server may reject the wrapped scheme on some versions per ArrCore's own comment.

No LAN discovery code (Bonjour/NWBrowser/NetService/mDNS/UDP broadcast) exists anywhere in ArrCore or the MediaKit spike — servers are configured by URL only, confirmed by an empty grep across both packages.

MediaKit's TMDBAuth.swift is a near-verbatim duplicate of TMDBClient's isReadAccessToken()/query-vs-Bearer logic — same prefix check ('eyJ' or 3-part JWT), same fallback to api_key query param — so the spike has not changed or improved the TMDB credential-handling behavior, only relocated it.

MediaKitBridge.swift in TonightCore is explicitly documented (its own header comment) as 'the whole migration surface' — TonightBarr's views still bind to the app-local MediaItem type, and MediaKit's MediaSnapshot/MediaIdentity are converted at this one seam. ArrBarr proper (ArrCore) does not import MediaKit at all today; only TonightCore (11 files) does.

MediaKit's identity vocabulary (MediaID/MediaIdentity, Identity/MediaID.swift) is a strict superset of ArrCore's two identity types combined (MediaRef for arr/search routing + MediaServerExternalKey for media-server matching), adding .season/.episode/.artist/.album kinds and a unified .server(flavor,id)/.arr(flavor,id) case — a stronger single-namespace design than ArrCore's two separate enums.
open_questions: Is PosterStore itself expected to move into MediaKit eventually (e.g. as a caching layer keyed by MediaKit's MediaID instead of raw URLs), or does it stay a presentation-tier ArrCore service permanently? The MediaKit spike has no image-byte cache today (FragmentCache caches MediaFragment metadata, not image data), so PosterStore has no direct successor to compare against.

MediaKit's MediaServerProvider auth-header discrepancy (Emby always gets the MediaBrowser-wrapped token, never a bare X-Emby-Token) — is this a known simplification for the TonightBarr-only spike scope, or a bug that needs fixing before MediaKit could replace ArrCore's JellyfinClient?

SeriesIdentityResolver's DemoMode.isActive gate returns nil (i.e. 'no identity resolved') in demo mode rather than substituting a mock — is that the intended demo behavior (identity-dependent features simply degrade), or should MediaKit's TMDBIdentityResolver add an explicit demo path?

TMDBClient's v3 api_key-in-query behavior for the JSON API endpoints is inherited unchanged into MediaKit's TMDBAuth — is there an intention to move every TMDB caller to v4 Bearer-only in the MediaKit migration, or must v3 hex keys keep working indefinitely?
summary: Read-only inventory of ArrCore's media-server (Plex/Jellyfin/Emby)/TMDB/poster/identity stack versus the MediaKit spike. All 8 MediaServerClient methods on both PlexClient and JellyfinClient authenticate via header only (X-Plex-Token / X-Emby-Token / MediaBrowser Authorization), never in a query string; only 2 of those methods mutate server state (scanLibrary via GET/POST, emptyTrash via PUT). TMDBClient's JSON API calls put a legacy v3 hex key in an api_key query parameter (v4 JWT keys go to an Authorization Bearer header instead) but TMDB image URLs never carry any credential. PosterStore's cache key is a SHA256 hash of the URL (not the raw URL), and the design already documents and defends against media-server tokens leaking into the poster URL/cache — no credential leak found in this codebase today. DemoMode.isActive gates only SeriesIdentityResolver's TMDB/Sonarr bridge (2 call sites); none of the media-server or TMDB client files check DemoMode at all. No LAN/Bonjour discovery code exists anywhere in scope. The MediaKit spike (18 source files, ~3459 LOC, 1011 LOC of tests) is a from-scratch, more general reimplementation (unified MediaID/MediaIdentity vocabulary, MediaGraph query planner, FragmentCache, per-provider MediaServerProvider/TMDBProvider/RadarrProvider/SonarrProvider) that TonightCore already imports and bridges to (MediaKitBridge.swift is explicitly the single migration seam); ArrCore itself does not import MediaKit yet. 9 ArrCore files totaling 2143 LOC (Plex/Jellyfin clients, the MediaServerClient protocol+factory+GuidParser, MediaServerIndex, MediaServerPosterAccess, MediaServerTypes DTOs, ArrMediaServerKeys, SeriesIdentityResolver, and TMDBClient) map onto MediaKit responsibilities; PosterStore, TMDBSearchMapping, LocalToolBackend+TMDB, NotificationArtwork, MediaRef, MediaServerConfig, and DiscoverItem stay ArrCore-side as presentation/domain composition. One correctness discrepancy was found: MediaKit's MediaServerProvider always wraps Jellyfin/Emby tokens in the 'MediaBrowser Token=' scheme, while ArrCore's shipping client sends Emby a bare X-Emby-Token — a gap to reconcile before MediaKit could replace JellyfinClient.
